Note · Shannon — A Mathematical Theory of Communication

4 min read913 wordsUpdated 2026-06-06notes/canon/canon-shannon-information-theory.md

Canon · Cluster: Information & Communication · Maps to Course 07 (Data & Decision-Making), E7 (Exec Presence & Comms)

  • Source: Claude Shannon, A Mathematical Theory of Communication (1948)
  • Core claim: Information is the reduction of uncertainty. A message is more informative the more surprising it is — and reliable communication over a noisy channel requires redundancy.
  • Framework:
  • Information = surprise — a perfectly predictable message carries zero information; entropy measures uncertainty/surprise.
  • Channel capacity — there's a hard limit to how much information a channel can reliably carry.
  • Noise corrupts messages; redundancy is error-correction, not waste — repeating / re-encoding the signal is how it survives the channel.
  • Leadership translation: most communication fails because the channel is noisy (distraction, competing messages, misunderstanding). The fix is intentional redundancy — say the important thing multiple ways through multiple channels. If you said it once, you haven't said it.
  • Applies when: any communication that must land — a strategy, a change message, a safety- critical instruction — across a noisy organization.
  • Breaks when: redundancy has a ceiling — past a point, repetition becomes noise itself (everything "urgent" = nothing urgent), and over-communication breeds tune-out. The math is about fidelity of transmission, not meaning, persuasion, or whether the idea is any good — a perfectly transmitted bad message is still bad (that's Minto/Sinek/Duarte's domain, canon minto pyramid principle). Don't over-literalize a 1948 engineering theorem into a theory of leadership.

  • Practitioner counterpoint: (researched 2026-06-06 — "Claude Shannon Explains Information Theory" transcript, youtube.com/watch?v=1afrzErFy_k) The book-specific re-pull surfaces Shannon in his own recorded words, and he draws the line the leadership translation glosses over: the 1948 math is deliberately about transmission, not meaning. "What I realized was, to measure information you have to look at it without regard to meaning — that upset a lot of people, that content is irrelevant." He defines the payload precisely: "the point of sending a message is to remove uncertainty — something you didn't know, now you know." The famous redundancy maxim leaders relearn — that you have to say a thing more than once before it lands — is just Shannon's error-correction in the wild, but the theorem only certifies the bits arrive, not that the idea was good. Bungay's alignment gap is the same redundancy idea in command language (canon bungay art of action).

  • Researched layer (updated 2026-06-06)

  • Canonical explanation (sourced): Shannon's core move is to strip meaning out so information can be measured like energy. In his own recorded words: "I wanted to try to find a way to treat information like a physical thing, like energy, that you could measure" and "to measure information you have to look at it without regard to meaning" ("Claude Shannon Explains Information Theory", youtube.com/watch?v=1afrzErFy_k). The unit is the bit — one fair coin toss: "a coin toss is an example of the simplest form of information… a true or false, heads or tails, a one or a zero, a bit." And the boundary conditions: "if something's completely predictable there's zero information, but if something's completely random you need information about everything."
  • The mechanism, verified across transcripts: entropy is the average surprise, and the Art of the Problem video reframes it operationally as the minimum number of yes/no questions you'd expect to ask. Two machines emit A/B/C/D: a uniform source needs 2 questions per symbol, but a skewed source (A 50%, D 25%, B/C 12.5%) needs only 1.75 — "Machine 2 is producing less information because there is less uncertainty or surprise about its output" ("Shannon's Information Entropy (Physical Analogy)", youtube.com/watch?v=R4OlXb9aTvQ). Shannon "calls this measure of average uncertainty 'entropy,' and he uses a letter H to represent it."
  • Real application (mined): the corpus grounds the theory in literal channel accounting, not metaphor: "if I toss it a hundred times… I'd need a hundred bits of information, one for each toss, to communicate the results" — but a rigged two-headed coin is fully predictable, so "I didn't need any information from you to know the results" (1afrzErFy_k). That is the redundancy / compression payoff stated as a hard count of bits, which is exactly why leaders must budget repetition for uncertain messages, not predictable ones.
  • Where the corpus pushes back on the book: Shannon's quantity is content-free — "that upset a lot of people, that content is irrelevant" (1afrzErFy_k). The math certifies that the bits survive the noisy channel; it says nothing about whether the message persuades or whether the idea is worth transmitting. That's exactly the note's "breaks-when": don't over-literalize a 1948 transmission theorem into a theory of meaning or leadership (canon minto pyramid principle).
  • Sources in corpus: "Claude Shannon Explains Information Theory" (youtube.com/watch?v=1afrzErFy_k) · Art of the Problem — "Shannon's Information Entropy (Physical Analogy)" (youtube.com/watch?v=R4OlXb9aTvQ) · Computerphile — "Why Information Theory is Important" (youtube.com/watch?v=b6VdGHSV6qg). Rep

Take your most important current message. Are you relying on a single channel (one email)? Re-send the same core idea through two more channels, worded differently. Assume it hasn't landed yet.

Marks itself read when you reach the end.
